warmup.text: Read Buffalo Dusk again. On Day 2 you named its elements. Today explain how they work together. Ask yourself what the poem would lose if every line were the same length.

words.text: Choose five words from across the year and use them in sentences about your theme. Then check roots, spellings and your own sentence types. The last four pairs finish the shelf.

reading.text: Read your own essay as if someone else wrote it. Answer the three reviewer questions. Then argue the other side: what would a reader who disagrees say, and how would you answer?

assignment.text: Pick two revision targets and make the changes. Paste your final essay, and note the two changes at the top. This is part one of your year-end portfolio.

readnow.text: No new chapter today. Review your essay as a reviewer, revise it twice, and submit.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you work. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Reading your own work as a stranger shows you what it really says.
how.use: You will use it in reviewer question 1.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one kind of mistake at a time catches more of them.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on.
how.why: Thinking first gives you something to watch for.

do: Read the poem out loud three times.
Read the tip.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Explaining how the parts work together is the last step of reading a poem well.

do: Read the word lists.
Choose five words from at least three novels.
Write about each one in the box.
how.why: This is your Show What You Know for vocabulary this week.

do: Answer the question in your reading journal.
Tap the right root for each word.
how.why: Roots let you read words you have never seen.

do: Type the right spelling of each word.
Tap Check My Work.
Check your own essay the same way.
how.why: The words you misspell most are the ones to check first.

do: Count your sentence types in your reading journal.
Read the before and after.
Tap the stronger sentence.
how.why: A comparison lives in sentences that connect two things.

do: Read your draft out loud.
Answer the three reviewer questions.
Argue the other side, then write what you learned this week.
how.why: Arguing the other side makes your own argument stronger.

do: Pick two revision targets.
Make the changes.
Paste the final essay, with the two changes noted at the top.
how.why: Two careful changes beat ten quick ones.

definitely: You can see finite inside it.

game.title: Two Books, One Root
game.sub: This week's word game · 4 pairs today
game.look: A bookshelf with this year's five novels, and one more book: You. Each card holds a word that belongs to one of those worlds. Two words with the same root are a pair. Find a pair and a gold thread ties their two worlds together.

do: Tap a card to turn it over.
Tap a second card.
Same root? The pair stays up. Different roots? They turn back over.
how.why: A root is the same in every book. Spotting it lets you read a word you have never seen.

game.miss: Look for the same few letters inside both words.
game.doneLine: Sixteen threads. Every book on the shelf is tied to another.

pairs.why: Nat's book began as a manuscript; a postscript is the P.S. written after a letter, like the one you write next week.
Perspective is where you look from, like Isaac's; to inspect is to look closely, like you at your draft today.
Bayard Taylor found that every man was his own porter in 1849 San Francisco; Salem ships carried goods out to export them.
Praiseworthy's win was hard to believe, incredible; giving credit to a source tells readers whom to believe.

virtue.name: wisdom
virtue.title: The wisest character of the year
virtue.intro: Look back at this year's novels. Tap the character you think acted most wisely.

options.t: Kit Tyler, who keeps visiting Hannah Tupper when the town turns against her (The Witch of Blackbird Pond).
Nat Bowditch, who checks every figure because sailors' lives depend on it (Carry On, Mr. Bowditch).
Praiseworthy, who keeps his word and comes back to fight the Mountain Ox (By the Great Horn Spoon!).
Isaac, who tells you on page one to be careful what you wish for (How I Became a Ghost).

virtue.line: Finish the sentence: This character was wise because…

art.title: Young Girl Reading
art.alt: A painting of a girl in a bright yellow dress sitting against a large pillow, holding a small open book in one hand and reading.
art.look: Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted this girl lost in a book around 1769. Look at how still she sits and how close she holds the page. This week you have been the reader too, across five novels.
